slides.heading: Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants: Pre-fertilisation
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how the male and female gametophytes are formed inside the flower.

visual.alt: Flow from the flower to its male and female reproductive whorls

slides.narration: The flower is the organ of sexual reproduction in angiosperms. Long before a flower opens, the decision to flower has been taken, and the floral buds develop. Inside them, the stamens and the pistil prepare the male and female gametophytes. This part follows how each one forms.

slides.heading: The two reproductive whorls
slides.body_md: A **stamen** has a slender **filament** and a terminal **anther**. A typical angiosperm anther is **bilobed** and **dithecous**: each lobe has two thecae, so the anther holds **four microsporangia**. The **pistil** has **stigma**, **style** and **ovary**; the ovary contains **ovules** attached to the **placenta**.

rows: Stigma, style, ovary with ovules on the placenta

visual.alt: Table of the male and female whorls with their parts

slides.narration: Think of the stamen as a stalk carrying a four-chambered bag of pollen, and the pistil as a landing platform, a tube and a chamber holding the ovules. A flower may have one pistil or many, free or fused.

slides.heading: Transverse section of the anther
slides.body_md: In T.S. the anther is **tetragonal**. Each **microsporangium** is surrounded by four wall layers: **epidermis**, **endothecium**, **middle layers** and **tapetum**. The centre holds **sporogenous tissue**.

slides.narration: The outer three layers protect the sporangium and help the anther to split open and release pollen. The innermost layer, the tapetum, feeds the developing pollen grains. Its cells have dense cytoplasm and often more than one nucleus.

slides.heading: Microsporogenesis
slides.body_md: Each cell of the sporogenous tissue can act as a **pollen mother cell (PMC)** or **microspore mother cell**. It divides by **meiosis** to form a **microspore tetrad**. As the anther matures and dehydrates, the microspores separate and develop into **pollen grains**.

visual.alt: Flow of microsporogenesis from sporogenous tissue to pollen grains

slides.narration: The process of forming microspores from a pollen mother cell by meiosis is called microsporogenesis. One mother cell gives four microspores, so every pollen grain carries a single set of chromosomes.

slides.heading: The pollen grain
slides.body_md: The pollen grain wall has a hard **exine** of **sporopollenin**, one of the most resistant organic materials known, with **germ pores** where sporopollenin is absent; and a thin **intine** of **cellulose and pectin**. A mature grain has a large **vegetative cell** and a small, spindle-shaped **generative cell**.

slides.narration: Sporopollenin withstands high temperature, strong acids and alkalis, and no known enzyme degrades it, which is why pollen is so well preserved as fossils. In over sixty percent of angiosperms pollen is shed at this two-celled stage; in the rest, the generative cell first divides into two male gametes.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: counting pollen and chromosomes
slides.body_md: An anther has 4 microsporangia, each with 30 pollen mother cells. The plant has 2n = 24. How many pollen grains form, and how many chromosomes does each microspore nucleus have?
bullets: Pollen mother cells $= 4 \times 30 = 120$.
Each meiosis gives 4 microspores: pollen $= 120 \times 4 = 480$.
Meiosis halves the number: microspore nucleus $= \dfrac{24}{2} = 12$ chromosomes.

visual.alt: Worked table: 480 pollen grains with 12 chromosomes each

slides.narration: Multiply the sporangia by the mother cells to get one hundred and twenty mother cells, and multiply by four because each meiosis gives a tetrad. That gives four hundred and eighty pollen grains. Each has half the parent number, twelve chromosomes.

slides.heading: Pollen viability and economic importance
slides.body_md: **Viability** is the period for which pollen remains able to germinate. It depends on the species and on temperature and humidity.

rows: Rice and wheat: about 30 minutes after release
Some members of Rosaceae, Leguminosae and Solanaceae: months
Pollen banks store pollen for years in liquid nitrogen at about −196 °C for crop breeding
Pollen of many species, such as Parthenium (carrot grass), causes asthma and bronchitis
Pollen tablets and syrups are marketed to improve health and athletic performance

visual.alt: Table of pollen viability and economic importance

slides.narration: Some pollen lives only for minutes, other pollen for months. Plant breeders store pollen in liquid nitrogen so that crosses can be made long after flowering. Pollen also matters to health, as an allergen and as a nutrient-rich supplement.

slides.heading: The pistil and the ovule
slides.body_md: An **ovule** is attached to the placenta by a stalk, the **funicle**, at the **hilum**. One or two **integuments** cover the **nucellus**, leaving an opening, the **micropyle**; the basal region opposite it is the **chalaza**. In an **anatropous** ovule, the body is inverted so the micropyle lies close to the funicle.

slides.narration: Inside the nucellus lies the embryo sac, the female gametophyte. Ovules usually have a single embryo sac formed from one megaspore. The number of ovules in an ovary may be one, as in wheat, paddy and mango, or many, as in papaya, watermelon and orchids.

slides.heading: Megasporogenesis
slides.body_md: A single **megaspore mother cell (MMC)** differentiates in the micropylar region of the nucellus. It divides by **meiosis** to give four megaspores. Usually **one is functional** and three degenerate. Development of the embryo sac from a single megaspore is **monosporic**.

visual.alt: Flow of megasporogenesis to the embryo sac

slides.narration: The functional megaspore nucleus divides by mitosis three times without forming walls, giving eight free nuclei. Only then do cell walls form. Free-nuclear division means nuclear division not followed at once by cell wall formation.

slides.heading: The mature embryo sac

slides.narration: The typical angiosperm embryo sac is therefore seven-celled and eight-nucleate. The filiform apparatus, a set of cellular thickenings at the tip of the synergids, guides the pollen tube into a synergid.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: nuclei and ploidy in the embryo sac
slides.body_md: The functional megaspore nucleus of a plant with 2n = 24 divides three times by free-nuclear mitosis. How many nuclei result, how many cells form, and what is the ploidy of each nucleus?
bullets: Cells: 3 antipodals + 2 synergids + 1 egg + 1 central cell = **7 cells** (the central cell has 2 polar nuclei).
All nuclei come from a haploid megaspore by mitosis, so each has $n = 12$ chromosomes.

visual.alt: Worked table: 7 cells, 8 nuclei, each with 12 chromosomes

slides.narration: Three rounds of doubling give eight nuclei. Six become separate cells and two share the central cell, so there are seven cells. Because mitosis copies the haploid megaspore nucleus, every one of these nuclei has twelve chromosomes.

slides.heading: Quick check: monosporic development
slides.body_md: How many megaspores take part in forming a monosporic embryo sac?
slides.narration: Quick check. Remember how many megaspores stay functional.

slides.heading: Quick check: embryo sac
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about the embryo sac.
slides.narration: Quick check. Count the cells and the nuclei separately.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Anther: bilobed, dithecous, four microsporangia; wall: epidermis, endothecium, middle layers, tapetum (nourishes).
Microsporogenesis: PMC → meiosis → microspore tetrad → pollen grains.
Pollen: exine of sporopollenin with germ pores; intine of cellulose and pectin; vegetative and generative cells.
Ovule: funicle, hilum, integuments, micropyle, chalaza, nucellus; anatropous.
Megasporogenesis: MMC → meiosis → 4 megaspores → 1 functional (monosporic) → 3 mitoses → 7 cells, 8 nuclei.

visual.alt: Summary table comparing male and female development

slides.narration: To recap: in the anther, pollen mother cells undergo meiosis to form pollen grains with a tough exine. In the ovule, one megaspore mother cell gives four megaspores, of which one forms the seven-celled, eight-nucleate embryo sac.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Draw the **T.S. of anther** and the **L.S. of an anatropous ovule** in pencil with neat label lines.
Give the **function of the tapetum** and the **reason exine survives** (sporopollenin).
State **monosporic** development and show the **8-nucleate, 7-celled** count.
Write ploidy correctly: PMC and MMC 2n; pollen, megaspore and all embryo-sac nuclei n.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Practise the anther and ovule diagrams in pencil. Know what the tapetum does and why exine lasts. Explain monosporic development. And write the ploidy of every cell correctly.

goals: Distinguish autogamy, chasmogamy, cleistogamy, geitonogamy and xenogamy
Relate floral adaptations to wind, water and insect pollination
Explain outbreeding devices and pollen–pistil interaction
Describe emasculation and bagging in artificial hybridisation

slides.heading: Pollination
slides.body_md: Part 2 — getting the pollen to the stigma, and the controls that decide which pollen succeeds.

nodes.label: Pollen tube grows to the ovule

visual.alt: Flow from pollen release to pollen tube growth

slides.narration: Male and female gametes are non-motile in flowering plants, so pollen must be brought to the stigma. This transfer is pollination. Plants have evolved many devices both to achieve it and to control which pollen is accepted.

slides.heading: Kinds of pollination
slides.body_md: **Autogamy**: pollen to the stigma of the same flower. **Geitonogamy**: to another flower of the **same plant** (functionally cross-pollination, but genetically like autogamy). **Xenogamy**: to the stigma of a **different plant**, bringing genetically different pollen.

slides.narration: Geitonogamy needs an agent to carry pollen between flowers, so it works like cross-pollination. But because the two flowers share one plant, the pollen is genetically the same, so the offspring are no more varied than with self-pollination. Only xenogamy brings new genes.

slides.heading: Chasmogamy and cleistogamy
slides.body_md: **Chasmogamous** flowers open, exposing anthers and stigma. **Cleistogamous** flowers never open; anthers and stigma lie close together, so pollen sheds directly on the stigma.

rows: Viola (pansy), Oxalis, Commelina (which also bear chasmogamous flowers)

visual.alt: Table comparing chasmogamous and cleistogamous flowers

slides.narration: Cleistogamous flowers guarantee seed even when pollinators are absent, but every seed comes from self-pollination. Plants such as Viola, Oxalis and Commelina hedge their bets by producing both kinds of flowers.

slides.heading: Wind and water pollination
slides.body_md: **Wind (anemophily)** is the commonest abiotic agent. **Water (hydrophily)** is rare, found in about 30 genera, mostly monocots.

rows: Light, non-sticky pollen in large numbers; well-exposed stamens; large, often feathery stigma; usually a single ovule per ovary; flowers packed in inflorescences; the familiar tassels of maize are stigmas and styles waving in the wind

Vallisneria, Hydrilla and the marine sea grass Zostera; in Vallisneria female flowers reach the surface on long stalks and released male flowers float to them; in sea grasses long, ribbon-like pollen is carried in the water and protected by a mucilaginous covering

visual.alt: Table of wind and water pollination adaptations with examples

slides.narration: Wind is wasteful, so wind-pollinated plants produce pollen in enormous quantities. Water pollination is rare. Note that not all aquatic plants use water: water hyacinth and water lily emerge above the surface and are pollinated by insects or wind.

slides.heading: Animal pollination
slides.body_md: Bees, butterflies, flies, beetles, wasps, ants, moths, birds (sunbirds, hummingbirds), bats and even some primates and reptiles act as pollinators. **Insects**, especially **bees**, are the dominant biotic agents.

rows: Large, colourful, fragrant flowers rich in nectar
Attract animals; small flowers clustered into an inflorescence
Amorphophallus, the tallest flower, gives a safe place to lay eggs; a moth species and Yucca cannot complete their life cycles without each other

visual.alt: Table of features of animal-pollinated flowers and their purposes

slides.narration: Animal-pollinated flowers advertise themselves with colour and scent and pay their visitors with nectar or pollen. Some visitors take nectar or pollen without pollinating; they are called pollen or nectar robbers.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: identify the agent
slides.body_md: Three flowers are described. Suggest the likely pollinating agent and give one reason for each.
bullets: Flower X: small, dull, no scent; feathery stigma; anthers on long filaments hanging out → **wind**: exposed anthers and feathery stigma.
Flower Y: large, bright, scented, with nectar; sticky pollen → **insect**: colour, scent and reward.
Flower Z: submerged plant; pollen ribbon-like with a mucilage coat → **water**: long pollen carried by currents.

visual.alt: Worked table matching three flowers to their pollinating agents

slides.narration: Look for the clues. Exposed anthers and a feathery stigma suit wind. Colour, scent, nectar and sticky pollen suit insects. A submerged plant with long, coated pollen grains suits water.

slides.heading: Quick check: agent
slides.body_md: Which feature suggests that a flower is wind-pollinated?
slides.narration: Quick check. Wind cannot be attracted by colour.

slides.heading: Self- versus cross-pollination
slides.body_md: Each mode has advantages.

rows: Needs no agent; seed set assured
Produces variation, the raw material for evolution
Offspring often more vigorous and adaptable
But continued selfing can cause inbreeding depression
But depends on agents and wastes more pollen

visual.alt: Table comparing advantages of self- and cross-pollination

slides.narration: Self-pollination is economical and reliable, but continued self-pollination leads to inbreeding depression. Cross-pollination costs more but produces varied, often more vigorous, offspring. Most flowering plants produce hermaphrodite flowers, so they have evolved devices to discourage self-pollination.

slides.heading: Outbreeding devices
slides.body_md: Devices that discourage self-pollination and encourage cross-pollination:

rows: Pollen release and stigma receptivity are not synchronised: protandry (anthers mature first) or protogyny (stigma first)
Anther and stigma placed at different positions, so pollen cannot reach the stigma of the same flower
A genetic mechanism prevents self-pollen (from the same flower or other flowers of the same plant) from germinating or growing in the pistil
Monoecious plants (castor, maize) prevent autogamy but not geitonogamy; dioecious plants (papaya) prevent both

visual.alt: Table of outbreeding devices and how they work

slides.narration: Timing, position, genetics and separation of the sexes all discourage self-pollination. Notice the difference between monoecious and dioecious plants: only when male and female flowers are on different plants is self-pollination of every kind prevented.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: which device stops which pollination?
slides.body_md: For each plant, state whether autogamy and geitonogamy are possible.
bullets: Castor (monoecious: male and female flowers on one plant): autogamy **not possible**; geitonogamy **possible**.
Papaya (dioecious: male and female plants): autogamy and geitonogamy **both not possible**; only xenogamy.
A self-incompatible hermaphrodite: pollen of the same plant **fails** in the pistil, so seed comes only from xenogamy.

visual.alt: Worked table of which kinds of pollination are possible in three plants

slides.narration: A unisexual flower cannot pollinate itself, so autogamy is ruled out. But if male and female flowers grow on the same plant, pollen can still move between them. Only separate male and female plants, or self-incompatibility, rule out both forms of self-pollination.

slides.heading: Quick check: outbreeding
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about monoecious plants.
slides.narration: Quick check. Can pollen move between flowers on the same plant?

slides.heading: Pollen–pistil interaction
slides.body_md: The pistil can **recognise** whether pollen is compatible. Compatible pollen is accepted and germinates; incompatible pollen is rejected by stopping germination on the stigma or tube growth in the style. Recognition depends on **chemical components** of the pollen interacting with those of the pistil.

nodes.label: Compatible: germinates through a germ pore
Pollen tube grows through stigma and style, carrying the cell contents
Enters ovule through micropyle; filiform apparatus guides it into a synergid
Incompatible: germination or tube growth blocked

visual.alt: Flow of pollen–pistil interaction

slides.narration: All the events from pollen landing on the stigma to the pollen tube entering the ovule are called pollen–pistil interaction. It is a dynamic, chemically controlled dialogue, and plant breeders use their understanding of it to make crosses that would otherwise fail.

slides.heading: Artificial hybridisation
slides.body_md: To cross chosen parents, breeders make sure that **only the desired pollen** reaches the stigma.

nodes.label: Emasculation: remove anthers from the bud of the bisexual female parent before they dehisce
Bagging: cover the flower with a butter-paper bag
When the stigma is receptive, dust it with pollen from the male parent
Rebag and allow fruit and seed to develop

visual.alt: Flow of emasculation and bagging in artificial hybridisation

slides.narration: Emasculation removes the flower’s own anthers so it cannot self-pollinate. Bagging keeps out unwanted pollen. If the female parent already has unisexual flowers, emasculation is not needed; the female buds are simply bagged. Hybridisation combines desirable characters, which is the basis of crop improvement.

slides.heading: Quick check: emasculation
slides.body_md: Why is emasculation done before the anthers dehisce?
slides.narration: Quick check. What would happen if the anthers had already released pollen?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Autogamy, geitonogamy (genetically like autogamy), xenogamy; chasmogamous and cleistogamous (Viola, Oxalis, Commelina) flowers.
Wind: light pollen, exposed stamens, feathery stigma, single ovule. Water: Vallisneria, Hydrilla, Zostera. Insects: colour, scent, nectar, sticky pollen; Amorphophallus; Yucca and its moth.
Outbreeding devices: dichogamy, herkogamy, self-incompatibility, unisexuality (monoecious castor and maize; dioecious papaya).
Pollen–pistil interaction: chemical recognition, germination, tube growth, entry via micropyle and synergid.
Artificial hybridisation: emasculation, bagging, pollination, rebagging.

visual.alt: Summary table of what three conditions prevent

slides.narration: To recap: flowers are adapted to their pollinating agents, and many have devices that favour cross-pollination. The pistil recognises compatible pollen, and breeders exploit all of this through emasculation and bagging.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Explain why **geitonogamy** is functionally cross- but genetically self-pollination.
Give **three adaptations** each for wind and insect pollination.
For outbreeding devices, give a **named example** where the syllabus has one.
**Give reasons** questions: answer in one precise sentence with the key term.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Be ready to explain geitonogamy. Learn three adaptations for each agent. Give named examples for outbreeding devices. And answer give-a-reason questions in one precise sentence that uses the key term.

notes.title: Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants: Pre-fertilisation — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Stamen, microsporangium and pollen grain
sections.body_md:
**Flower.** The site of sexual reproduction in angiosperms. The **androecium** (whorl of stamens) is the male reproductive organ and the **gynoecium** (pistil) the female.

**Stamen.** A long, slender **filament** and a terminal, usually **bilobed** anther. Each lobe has two **thecae** (dithecous), so a typical anther is **tetrasporangiate**: four **microsporangia** at the corners, which develop into **pollen sacs**.

**Wall of the microsporangium** (outside to inside):
- **Epidermis** — protection.
- **Endothecium** — fibrous thickenings help in **dehiscence** of the anther.
- **Middle layers** (two or three) — protection; degenerate later.
- **Tapetum** — innermost; **nourishes** the developing pollen grains; cells have dense cytoplasm and usually **more than one nucleus**.

**Microsporogenesis.** Cells of the **sporogenous tissue** act as **pollen (microspore) mother cells, PMC (2n)**. Each divides by **meiosis** to form a **microspore tetrad (n)**. As the anther matures and dehydrates, the microspores dissociate and develop into **pollen grains**.

**Pollen grain.** Usually spherical, 25–50 µm across, with two wall layers:
- **Exine** of **sporopollenin**, one of the most resistant organic materials known: it withstands high temperatures and strong acids and alkalis, and no enzyme is known to degrade it — so pollen is well preserved as **fossils**. **Germ pores** are apertures where sporopollenin is absent.
- **Intine**: thin, continuous, of **cellulose and pectin**.

The mature pollen grain contains a large **vegetative cell** (abundant food reserve, large irregular nucleus) and a small, spindle-shaped **generative cell** floating in its cytoplasm. In **over 60 percent** of angiosperms pollen is shed at this **2-celled** stage; in the rest, the generative cell divides mitotically to give **two male gametes** before shedding (**3-celled** stage).

**Viability and economic importance.**
- Viability: about **30 minutes** in rice and wheat; **months** in some members of Rosaceae, Leguminosae and Solanaceae.
- **Pollen banks**: pollen stored for years in **liquid nitrogen (about −196 °C)** for crop-breeding programmes.
- **Allergy**: pollen of many species (e.g. **Parthenium**, carrot grass, which came to India as a contaminant with imported wheat) causes chronic respiratory disorders such as asthma and bronchitis.
- **Food supplements**: pollen is rich in nutrients; pollen tablets and syrups are marketed.

key_terms.definition_md: A pollen sac of the anther; a typical anther has four.
The innermost wall layer of the microsporangium, which nourishes the developing pollen grains.
Formation of microspores from a pollen mother cell by meiosis.

sections.heading: 2. Pistil, megasporangium and embryo sac
sections.body_md:
**Pistil.** Stigma (landing platform for pollen), style (elongated slender part) and ovary (swollen base). Inside the ovary cavity (**locule**) ovules arise from the **placenta**. A gynoecium may be **monocarpellary** or **multicarpellary**, with carpels free (**apocarpous**, e.g. Michelia) or fused (**syncarpous**, e.g. Papaver).

**Ovule (megasporangium).** Attached to the placenta by the **funicle**; the junction of ovule and funicle is the **hilum**. One or two protective **integuments** cover the ovule except at the **micropyle**. Opposite the micropyle is the **chalaza**, the basal part. The **nucellus**, a mass of cells with abundant food reserve, is enclosed by the integuments; it contains the **embryo sac** (female gametophyte). The common angiosperm ovule is **anatropous** (inverted).

**Megasporogenesis.** One **megaspore mother cell (MMC, 2n)**, large with dense cytoplasm and a prominent nucleus, differentiates in the **micropylar region** of the nucellus. It undergoes **meiosis** to form **four megaspores (n)**. In most flowering plants **one is functional** and **three degenerate**. Formation of the embryo sac from a **single megaspore** is called **monosporic** development.

**Female gametophyte.** The nucleus of the functional megaspore divides **mitotically** to form two nuclei, which move to opposite poles (**2-nucleate** embryo sac). Two more **free-nuclear** divisions at each pole give **4-nucleate** and then **8-nucleate** stages; cell walls form only after the 8-nucleate stage.
- **Micropylar end:** the **egg apparatus** — two **synergids** and one **egg cell**. Synergids have **filiform apparatus**, special cellular thickenings that guide the pollen tube into a synergid.
- **Chalazal end:** three **antipodals**.
- **Centre:** the large **central cell** with **two polar nuclei**.
So a typical mature embryo sac is **8-nucleate and 7-celled**. All its nuclei are **haploid**.

sections.heading: 3. Pollination: kinds and agencies
sections.body_md:
**Pollination** is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of a pistil.

**Kinds by source of pollen:**
- **Autogamy** — to the stigma of the **same flower**. Complete autogamy is rare in open flowers, as it needs synchrony of pollen release and stigma receptivity and close anthers and stigma. **Chasmogamous** flowers have exposed anthers and stigma; **cleistogamous** flowers never open, so they are invariably autogamous and give **assured seed set** even without pollinators (e.g. **Viola** (common pansy), **Oxalis**, **Commelina**, which produce both kinds).
- **Geitonogamy** — to another flower of the **same plant**: functionally cross-pollination (involves an agent) but **genetically similar to autogamy**.
- **Xenogamy** — to the stigma of a **different plant**: brings **genetically different** pollen.

**Agencies.**
- **Wind (anemophily):** light, non-sticky pollen produced in large numbers; well-exposed stamens; large, often feathery stigma to trap pollen; usually a **single ovule** in each ovary; numerous flowers packed into an inflorescence (the corn cob’s **tassels** are stigmas and styles); common in grasses.
- **Water (hydrophily):** rare, about **30 genera**, mostly monocots: **Vallisneria**, **Hydrilla** (fresh water), **Zostera** (marine sea grass). In **Vallisneria** female flowers reach the surface on long stalks and male flowers, released on the surface, are carried passively to them. In sea grasses, female flowers stay submerged and **long, ribbon-like** pollen grains are carried in the water; pollen of water-pollinated species has a **mucilaginous** covering against wetting. Not all aquatic plants use water: water hyacinth and water lily are pollinated by insects or wind.
- **Animals (zoophily):** bees, butterflies, flies, beetles, wasps, ants, moths, birds (sunbirds, hummingbirds), bats, some primates and reptiles. Insects, especially **bees**, dominate. Flowers are **large, colourful, fragrant** and rich in **nectar**; small flowers are clustered. Pollen is generally **sticky**. **Floral rewards** are nectar and pollen. **Amorphophallus** (tallest flower, about 6 feet) and **Yucca** with its moth show flowers that offer **safe places to lay eggs**. **Pollen/nectar robbers** consume rewards without pollinating.

**Advantages.** Self-pollination: needs no agent, seed set assured, maintains purity of line, less waste of pollen. Cross-pollination: produces **genetic variation**, healthier and more vigorous offspring, and adaptability; continued self-pollination results in **inbreeding depression**.

sections.heading: 4. Outbreeding devices, pollen–pistil interaction and artificial hybridisation
sections.body_md:
**Outbreeding devices** (contrivances that discourage self-pollination):
1. **Dichogamy** — pollen release and stigma receptivity are **not synchronised**: **protandry** (anthers mature first) or **protogyny** (stigma receptive first).
2. **Herkogamy** — anther and stigma are placed at **different positions**, so pollen cannot reach the stigma of the same flower.
3. **Self-incompatibility** — a **genetic** mechanism that prevents self-pollen (from the same flower or other flowers of the same plant) from **germinating** or its tube from **growing** in the pistil.
4. **Unisexual flowers** — **monoecious** plants (male and female flowers on the same plant: **castor, maize**) prevent **autogamy but not geitonogamy**; **dioecious** plants (male and female flowers on different plants: **papaya**) prevent **both**.

**Pollen–pistil interaction.** Pollination does not guarantee the right pollen. The pistil **recognises** compatible pollen of the same species and **rejects** the rest by preventing germination on the stigma or tube growth in the style. Recognition is mediated by **chemical components** of the pollen interacting with those of the pistil. Compatible pollen germinates to produce a **pollen tube** through one of the **germ pores**; the contents of the pollen grain move into the tube, which grows through the stigma and style to reach the ovary. In plants that shed 2-celled pollen, the generative cell divides into two male gametes during tube growth. The tube enters the ovule through the **micropyle** and then a **synergid**, guided by the **filiform apparatus**. All events from pollen deposition to tube entry are **pollen–pistil interaction**; understanding them helps breeders manipulate crosses, even incompatible ones.

**Artificial hybridisation** — crossing chosen parents in crop improvement:
- **Emasculation**: removing the anthers from the flower **bud** of a bisexual female parent **before** they dehisce, using forceps.
- **Bagging**: covering the emasculated flower with a bag of suitable size, usually **butter paper**, to prevent contamination by unwanted pollen.
- When the stigma becomes **receptive**, mature pollen from the chosen male parent is dusted on it, and the flower is **rebagged** to let the fruit develop.
- If the female parent bears **unisexual flowers**, emasculation is not needed: female buds are simply bagged before they open.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Calling the tapetum the outermost layer (it is the innermost and nourishes pollen).
- Writing that exine covers the germ pores (germ pores lack sporopollenin).
- Saying the embryo sac has eight cells (it has seven cells and eight nuclei).
- Calling geitonogamy genetic cross-pollination.
- Saying monoecy prevents geitonogamy (only dioecy does).
- Forgetting that emasculation is done in the bud, before dehiscence.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark subparts: a term, a reason in one sentence, an example, an option.
- 2–3-mark questions: labelled diagram (anther T.S., pollen grain, ovule L.S., embryo sac); differences between pairs; steps of a process.
- 5-mark questions in parts: microsporogenesis or megasporogenesis with a diagram; agencies with adaptations; outbreeding devices with examples; artificial hybridisation.
- Diagrams: drawn in pencil, label lines horizontal and not crossing, labels on one side.

questions.solution_md: The innermost layer, the tapetum, nourishes the developing pollen grains — option (b).

questions.solution_md: The endothecium, below the epidermis, helps in dehiscence — option (b).

The generative cell secretes a protective wax.
Pollen grains are coated with mucilage.
The exine contains sporopollenin, which resists high temperature, strong acids and alkalis, and no known enzyme degrades it.

questions.solution_md: Sporopollenin in the exine is one of the most resistant organic materials known, so pollen fossilises well — option (d).

questions.stem_md: When a pollen grain germinates, the pollen tube always emerges at particular points on its surface. Why?

options.text_md: These points have the thickest exine.
The generative cell pushes through the thinnest intine anywhere.

questions.solution_md: Germ pores lack sporopollenin, so the tube can push out there — option (d).

questions.solution_md: Most angiosperms shed pollen with a vegetative and a generative cell; the rest shed it at the 3-celled stage — option (b).

questions.solution_md: Parthenium pollen is a common allergen — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
(a) Describe the wall layers of a microsporangium, stating one function each of the endothecium and the tapetum. [2]
(b) Describe microsporogenesis and the development of the pollen grain up to the two-celled stage. [2]
(c) Give one economic importance of pollen grains. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) From outside in, the wall has the **epidermis**, **endothecium**, two or three **middle layers** and the **tapetum**. The **endothecium** has fibrous thickenings that help the anther to **dehisce**; the **tapetum**, with dense cytoplasm and often more than one nucleus, **nourishes** the developing pollen grains.

(b) The centre of a young microsporangium has **sporogenous tissue**. Its cells act as **pollen mother cells (2n)**, each of which divides by **meiosis** to form a **tetrad of four haploid microspores**. As the anther dehydrates, the microspores separate and each develops a wall of **exine** (sporopollenin, with germ pores) and **intine** (cellulose and pectin). The microspore nucleus divides by **mitosis** to form a large **vegetative cell** and a small **generative cell**: the **two-celled pollen grain**.

(c) Pollen is stored in **pollen banks** for crop breeding (or: pollen tablets are used as **food supplements**; pollen of some plants such as **Parthenium** causes allergies).

questions.solution_md: Wall layers with functions; microsporogenesis; one importance.

questions.stem_md: Describe megasporogenesis and explain what is meant by monosporic development of the embryo sac.

answer.model_answer_md: A single large **megaspore mother cell (2n)**, with dense cytoplasm and a prominent nucleus, differentiates in the **micropylar region** of the **nucellus**. questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of the L.S. of an anatropous ovule. [2]
(b) Describe the development of the female gametophyte from the functional megaspore. [2]
(c) A student says, “The female gametophyte has eight cells.” Correct the statement. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Labels:** funicle, hilum, outer and inner integuments, micropyle, chalaza, nucellus and embryo sac, with the micropyle lying close to the funicle (inverted ovule).

(b) The nucleus of the **functional megaspore** divides by mitosis into two nuclei, which move to opposite poles (2-nucleate embryo sac). Two further **free-nuclear** mitoses at each pole give the **4-nucleate** and then the **8-nucleate** stage. Cell walls then form: three cells at the micropylar end make the **egg apparatus** (two **synergids** and an **egg cell**), three at the chalazal end are **antipodals**, and the two remaining **polar nuclei** stay in the large **central cell**.

(c) The female gametophyte has **eight nuclei but seven cells**, because the two polar nuclei share one central cell.

answer.model_answer_md: Wind carries pollen **randomly**, so most of it is **wasted**; large numbers ensure that some reach a stigma.

questions.solution_md: Wastage in random transfer.

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: Cleistogamous flowers are invariably autogamous.

answer.model_answer_md: They **never open**, so pollen from their anthers can reach only their **own stigma**.

questions.solution_md: Closed flower.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between geitonogamy and xenogamy, stating which one brings genetic variation.

answer.model_answer_md: **Geitonogamy** is transfer of pollen to another flower of the **same plant**; it needs an agent but the pollen is **genetically the same**. **Xenogamy** is transfer to a flower of a **different plant**, bringing **genetically different pollen**, so only **xenogamy** produces genetic variation.

questions.solution_md: Source of pollen; variation.

questions.stem_md: Give two advantages of self-pollination and two of cross-pollination.

answer.model_answer_md: **Self-pollination:** **seed set is assured** without any agent; it **maintains pure lines** and wastes little pollen. **Cross-pollination:** it produces **genetic variation** and **more vigorous, adaptable offspring**, avoiding inbreeding depression.

questions.solution_md: Two each.

questions.stem_md: A gardener grows a single isolated tree of a self-compatible species and finds that bees visit its many flowers. Explain why its seedlings show little genetic variation even though insects pollinated the flowers.

answer.model_answer_md: With only one tree, bees carry pollen **between flowers of the same plant**: **geitonogamy**. Although an agent is involved, the pollen is **genetically identical** to the ovules’ parent, so it is **genetically equivalent to self-pollination** and gives little variation.

questions.solution_md: Geitonogamy is genetically selfing.

questions.stem_md: Compare wind-pollinated and insect-pollinated flowers in respect of (i) the pollen, (ii) the stigma and (iii) the corolla and nectar.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Pollen:** wind — **light, dry, non-sticky** and produced in **huge numbers**; insect — **sticky** and fewer.

(ii) **Stigma:** wind — **large, often feathery**, well exposed; insect — usually **sticky** and within the flower.

(iii) **Corolla and nectar:** wind — flowers small, **dull, unscented**, no nectar; insect — **large, colourful, fragrant**, with **nectar** as a reward.

questions.solution_md: Three comparisons.

questions.stem_md: Describe how pollination takes place in (i) Vallisneria and (ii) a marine sea grass such as Zostera. Why is water pollination rare?

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Vallisneria:** female flowers reach the **water surface** on **long stalks**; male flowers or pollen are released on the surface and **carried passively** by currents, some reaching the female flowers.

(ii) **Sea grasses:** female flowers stay **submerged**; **long, ribbon-like** pollen grains, protected by **mucilage**, are carried **inside the water** to the stigmas.

Water pollination is rare (about **30 genera**, mostly monocots) because most flowers are borne above water, where wind and animals are more efficient carriers.

questions.solution_md: Two mechanisms; rarity.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Distinguish between chasmogamous and cleistogamous flowers, naming one plant that bears both. [2]
(b) Explain how a flower such as Amorphophallus or Yucca benefits its pollinator besides offering nectar. [1]
(c) A farmer finds that a crop gives poor seed set in a year when bees are scarce, while a weed nearby sets seed normally. Suggest one floral feature of the weed that could explain this, and its disadvantage. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Chasmogamous** flowers **open**, exposing anthers and stigma, so they can be self- or cross-pollinated. **Cleistogamous** flowers **never open**; anthers and stigma lie close together, so they are always **autogamous**. **Commelina** (also Viola, Oxalis) bears both.

(b) These flowers offer the insect a **safe place to lay eggs**; in Yucca the moth’s larvae develop in the ovary, while the moth pollinates the flower.

(c) The weed may bear **cleistogamous flowers**, which self-pollinate without any agent and so give **assured seed set** when bees are scarce. Their disadvantage is that seeds come only from **self-pollination**, so the offspring have **little genetic variation** (and may suffer inbreeding depression).

questions.solution_md: Chasmogamy and cleistogamy; egg-laying site; assured seed set versus variation.

questions.stem_md: A plant species prevents both autogamy and geitonogamy. Which condition does it most likely show?
questions.solution_md: Only when male and female flowers are on different plants are both forms of self-pollination prevented — option (d).

options.text_md: the anthers release pollen before the stigma becomes receptive
the stigma becomes receptive before the anthers mature

questions.solution_md: Protandry is a form of dichogamy in which the anthers mature first — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In a certain flower, the stigma projects far beyond the anthers so that its own pollen cannot fall on it. This outbreeding device is
questions.solution_md: Placing anther and stigma at different positions is herkogamy — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Pollen of a plant lands on its own stigma at the right time but fails to germinate, while pollen from another plant of the species germinates normally. This is due to

options.text_md: the absence of a germ pore
self-incompatibility, a genetic mechanism recognised through chemical components of pollen and pistil

questions.solution_md: Self-incompatibility prevents self-pollen from germinating or growing in the pistil — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Monoecious plants such as maize prevent both autogamy and geitonogamy.

**Reason (R):** In monoecious plants, male and female flowers are borne on different plants.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Monoecious plants bear male and female flowers on the same plant, so they prevent autogamy but not geitonogamy. Both statements are false — option (d).

questions.stem_md: What is meant by pollen–pistil interaction? On what does the pistil’s ability to recognise compatible pollen depend?

answer.model_answer_md: Pollen–pistil interaction is the series of events from the **deposition of pollen on the stigma** until the **pollen tube enters the ovule**. The pistil recognises compatible pollen through the interaction of **chemical components** of the pollen with those of the pistil.

questions.solution_md: Definition and chemical basis.

marking_scheme.step: Chemical components of pollen and pistil

questions.stem_md: Most flowering plants have bisexual flowers, yet many avoid self-pollination. Describe three devices that discourage self-pollination.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Dichogamy:** pollen release and stigma receptivity are **not synchronised** — anthers mature first (**protandry**) or the stigma does (**protogyny**).
2. **Herkogamy:** **anther and stigma** are placed at **different positions**, so pollen cannot reach the stigma of the same flower.
3. **Self-incompatibility:** a **genetic** mechanism stops self-pollen from **germinating** or its tube from **growing** in the pistil.

questions.solution_md: Three devices.

questions.stem_md: Why is emasculation carried out before the anthers dehisce?

options.text_md: To prevent the flower’s own pollen from reaching its stigma
To increase the number of ovules
To help the anthers release pollen

questions.solution_md: Removing anthers before they shed pollen prevents self-pollination of the female parent — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A breeder uses a maize plant as the female parent in a cross. Which step of artificial hybridisation can she skip?

options.text_md: Bagging, because maize pollen is heavy
Emasculation, because the female flowers are unisexual
Rebagging, because maize seeds form instantly

questions.solution_md: In unisexual female flowers there are no anthers to remove; the female buds only need bagging — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Emasculated flowers are usually covered with bags made of ______ paper to prevent contamination by unwanted pollen.
questions.solution_md: Butter paper.

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: An emasculated flower is rebagged after it has been dusted with the desired pollen.

answer.model_answer_md: To keep out **unwanted pollen** while the fruit and seeds develop.

questions.solution_md: Prevent contamination.

questions.stem_md: A breeder wants to combine high yield from variety P (bisexual flowers) with disease resistance from variety Q. Describe the steps she should follow, using P as the female parent.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Emasculation:** remove the **anthers** from flower **buds** of **P** with forceps **before they dehisce**.
2. **Bagging:** cover the emasculated buds with **butter-paper bags** to keep out unwanted pollen.
3. When the **stigma becomes receptive**, dust it with **pollen from Q**, then **rebag** the flower and let the fruit and seeds develop; the seeds give hybrid plants to be screened for both characters.

questions.solution_md: Emasculation, bagging, pollination and rebagging.

marking_scheme.step: Dusting Q pollen at receptivity and rebagging

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is the significance of artificial hybridisation in plant breeding? [1]
(b) Describe emasculation and bagging, explaining why each is necessary. [2]
(c) A breeder emasculated flowers of a bisexual variety but forgot to bag them. Predict two possible outcomes for the seeds formed, with reasons. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) It allows breeders to **combine desirable characters** of two parents (such as yield and resistance) in one variety, which is the basis of **crop improvement**.

(b) **Emasculation** is removal of the **anthers** from a **bud** of the bisexual female parent **before dehiscence**, so that its **own pollen** cannot pollinate it. **Bagging** is covering the emasculated flower with a **butter-paper bag** so that **no unwanted pollen** reaches the stigma; only the chosen pollen is dusted on it later.

(c) The open flowers could receive **pollen from other plants** carried by wind or insects. Some seeds may then be **hybrids with an unknown male parent**, and some flowers may set **no seed** if no pollen arrives; either way the cross would not be the one intended.

questions.solution_md: Significance; steps; prediction.

marking_scheme.step: (c) Possible failure of seed set or wrong hybrids

| P | Male and female flowers on the same plant; tassels of long styles hang out in the wind |
